name: Time perception
statement: How long something felt and how long it is remembered as lasting are produced by different processes, and under load they move in opposite directions.
meaning: There is no organ for duration, so a duration judgement has to be built from something else. Which something else depends on whether the person knew the judgement was coming. Told in advance, they attend to time as it passes, and anything that takes attention away shortens the interval. Asked by surprise afterwards, they reconstruct the interval from what they can retrieve about it, and a busy interval reconstructs as long. Psychologists call the first the prospective paradigm and the second the retrospective paradigm. The distinction is the engine behind three popular claims: that a holiday flies past and then looks long in hindsight, that years pass faster with age, and that time slows down in an emergency. Each of those claims has been measured. The measurements do not all say what the claims say.

origin.who: Richard A. Block and Dan Zakay
origin.note: Their meta-analysis of 20 experiments established the prospective and retrospective paradigms as producing different judgements rather than two measures of one thing. The folk claims are older. William James put the shrinking year down to recollection in 1890, in chapter XV of The Principles of Psychology at page 625. The name 'holiday paradox' is widely credited to Claudia Hammond's Time Warped, and no document fetched for this entry carries that attribution or the phrase.

evidence: Block and Zakay pooled 20 experiments from 16 references, median publication year 1985. Eighteen gave an effect size for the paradigm comparison. Prospective judgements were larger, weighted mean d+ = 0.35, 95% CI 0.26 to 0.43, with the mean duration judgement ratio 16% higher in the prospective paradigm. The mean coefficient of variation was 15% greater for retrospective judgements. Processing difficulty moderated the gap and did so on one side only: prospective ratios fell from 0.94 to 0.82 to 0.73 as processing went from easy to moderate to difficult, while retrospective ratios went 0.78, 0.76, 0.67 and did not differ reliably. Block, Hancock and Zakay later pooled 117 experiments from 85 publications on cognitive load. The two paradigms came apart cleanly. Under a random-effects model the prospective effect was d+ = -0.46, 95% CI -0.55 to -0.37, across 90 experiments, and the retrospective effect was d+ = +0.26, 95% CI +0.03 to +0.49, across 32. Neither load nor paradigm gave a main effect, F(1,111) = 2.25 and 0.21, and their interaction gave F(1,111) = 40.74, p < .001. Funnel plots, Begg and Mazumdar's test and failsafe Ns of 9,038 and 273 gave no sign of publication bias. Avni-Babad and Ritov ran the dissociation directly on routine. Ninety-three students worked through 20 rows of 38 symbols, counting how often an underlined symbol appeared in each row. The underlined symbol was X throughout in the routine condition and different in every row in the other. Neither main effect reached F = 1. The interaction was F(1,89) = 12.73, p = .001, eta squared .125. Routine was remembered as shorter, F(1,89) = 4.96, p = .03, and estimated as longer while it was happening, F(1,89) = 7.79, p = .006. On ageing, Block, Zakay and Hancock pooled 16 experiments in which younger and older adults judged brief intervals. Fourteen gave an effect size, all between-subjects, none longitudinal. The weighted mean was d+ = 0.40, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.52, and the ratio of subjective to objective duration was 21% higher in older adults, which the authors call the opposite direction from what is usually predicted. Method split it: production d+ = 0.60 over nine effect sizes, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.76, verbal estimation d+ = 0.27 over four, 95% CI 0.05 to 0.48, and reproduction d+ = -0.02 over three, 95% CI -0.31 to 0.27. Slope of the function relating judged to target duration showed no age effect, d+ = 0.04, 95% CI -0.29 to 0.37. On fear, Stetson, Fiesta and Eagleman winched volunteers 46 metres up a Suspended Catch Air Device tower and released them backwards for a 31-metre fall lasting 2.49 seconds. Seven of them used a stopwatch to mark out the duration twice, once after watching someone else take the fall and once from memory of their own. Estimates rose by 36%, from 2.17 plus or minus 0.24 seconds to 2.96 plus or minus 0.51, p < 0.03 on a one-tailed paired t test. During the fall the same people read digits off a wrist-worn display alternating with its own negative 6 milliseconds faster than their measured threshold. A 36% gain in temporal resolution would have predicted 79% accuracy. In-flight accuracy was far below that and no different from a ground control.

examples.tag: The queue watched and the queue recalled
examples.text: Waiting at a counter with nothing to do, a man watches the minutes and they crawl. Asked a week later how long he stood there, he has almost nothing to retrieve and reports a short wait. Attending to time lengthens it as it passes and leaves little to rebuild it from.

examples.tag: The first week in a new job
examples.text: A week of new faces, new rooms and new systems goes past quickly while it is happening and comes back as a long stretch when it is recalled. The two judgements are assembled from different materials, so a single crowded week can run short in one and long in the other.

examples.tag: The drive that leaves no trace
examples.text: A familiar route driven while thinking about something else takes no attention, and the driver pulls up with no sense of how long it took. Nothing was stored to reconstruct the interval from, and the journey is remembered as brief.

replication.headline: The split between felt and remembered duration is one of the better replicated results in the field. The three popular biases built on it fare worse, and the ageing one is close to nothing.
replication.detail: Block, Hancock and Zakay's 117 experiments put the load effect at d+ = -0.46 for prospective judgements and +0.26 for retrospective ones, opposite signs with non-overlapping intervals. Tobin, Bisson and Grondin took the same comparison out of the laboratory, timing 116 gamers through video game sessions of 12, 35 or 58 minutes in two gaming centres in Quebec City. Prospective estimates ran longer, ratio 1.375 against 1.115, F(1,110) = 7.919, p < .05, partial eta squared .067. Both ratios sat above 1, so both paradigms overestimated, against the authors' own prediction. Variability did not split the way Block and Zakay's pooling did: the Weber fraction gave F(1,110) = 0.010, p > .05. Ageing is the strand that does not survive. Wittmann and Lehnhoff interviewed 499 people aged 14 to 94 in Germany and Austria and reported effects accounting for at most 10% of variance. Friedman and Janssen ran the same six questions on 1,865 adults aged 16 to 80 in New Zealand and the Netherlands. In their 99-person laboratory sample the young and old groups did not differ on the composite scale, t(96) = 0.32, p = .75, d = 0.06, 95% CI -0.33 to 0.46. In their 1,766-person Dutch sample age correlated with the composite at r = .12, 95% CI .07 to .17, which they put at about 1% of variance. Only the question about the previous 10 years showed more, r = .21, 95% CI .17 to .26, and they put that at about 4%. A four-item scale about rushing and having too much to do correlated at r = .32, 95% CI .28 to .36, which they put at 10.0% of variance and call more than seven times as strong as age. In the Dutch sample 78.7% of responses on the six speed-of-time items were 'fast' or 'very fast' and 3.2% were 'slow' or 'very slow'. Friedman and Janssen also tested two proposed mechanisms. Feeding people false feedback that they had misdated news events shifted their self-reported telescoping hard, F(1,95) = 49.62, partial eta squared .34, and left the speed of time untouched. Answering thirty questions about news events of the past two years before rating the speed of time moved the composite the opposite way from the prediction and only approached significance, t(1764) = 1.77, p = .08, and the sample was large enough to reject any d above 0.03 in the predicted direction. Droit-Volet and Wearden sampled 27 people, 14 students and 13 older adults, by eight phone alerts a day for five days, and found no age difference in how fast time was judged to be passing, 4.75 against 4.49, p = 0.38. Fear is contested. Sarigiannidis and colleagues used threat of shock in three experiments; induced anxiety made people underestimate durations, with a meta-analytic effect the abstract and discussion give as d = 0.68 and the results section as d = 0.67, both with 95% CI 0.42 to 0.94. Two further experiments tried to reproduce the reported overestimation under fear. Study 4 shifted in the predicted direction without reaching significance, t(24) = 1.99, p = .058, d = 0.40, and the better-powered Study 5 found nothing, t(34) = 0.41, p = .687, d = 0.06.

study.cite: Block, R. A., Hancock, P. A., & Zakay, D. (2010). How cognitive load affects duration judgments: A meta-analytic review. Acta Psychologica, 134(3), 330-343.

limits: The verdict covers duration judgements and the paradigm distinction. It does not cover judgements of how fast time seems to be flowing, which Wearden argues should be distinguished from duration judgements, with the relation between the two remaining to be identified. Droit-Volet and Wearden sampled such judgements by phone alerts during ordinary life and found them predicted by happiness, sadness and how far the current activity captured attention, while verbal estimates and productions of 500, 1,000 and 1,500 milliseconds predicted nothing. Almost every experiment in the 1998 ageing meta-analysis used the prospective paradigm, on the authors' own statement, so it says little about remembered duration in older adults, and none of its 14 effect sizes came from a longitudinal design. The free-fall experiment rests on seven people for the duration judgement, and no direct replication of it was located. Its own text disagrees on two points: the fall is 31 metres in the abstract and methods and 50 metres in the discussion, and the in-flight against ground comparison is p = 0.98 in the results and p = 0.86 in the figure legend. Arstila disputes its reading, arguing that the experiment does not address the comprehensively altered experience accident survivors describe, and defending a realist account in which cognitive processing is rapidly enhanced. Droit-Volet's study of people over and under 75 found the current passage of time slowing rather than accelerating after 75, with sadness the best predictor, except among those whose cognitive functions had declined, who reported time passing quickly again. Whether the holiday paradox has been tested in the form it is usually stated could not be established. The nearest field data are Avni-Babad and Ritov's 41 Club Med guests in Eilat, and they concern parts of a holiday rather than the holiday against its memory: 51% named the last part of their stay as the shortest and 12% the first, chi-squared(2, N = 41) = 9.56, p < .01, with mean speed ratings of 3.54, 4.10 and 4.37 across the three parts on a five-point scale where 5 is fast. Hammond's Time Warped was not obtained, and the publisher's catalogue page describes it without using the phrase 'holiday paradox'. The 1% and 9% figures often quoted from Wittmann and Lehnhoff are taken here from Friedman and Janssen's description of that paper, not from the paper itself, which was read only as an abstract. Three sources were read as abstracts only: Wittmann and Lehnhoff, Wearden 2015 and Droit-Volet 2019. On 21 September 2026 the search for full text ran across Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, PMC, OpenAlex, Unpaywall, HAL, archive.org, PLOS, SpringerLink, Frontiers, SAGE, ScienceDirect and the authors' own posted copies.
misreadings: Popular writing treats prospective and retrospective judgements as one measurement, which is the thing the literature is most sure they are not. The whole holiday story depends on them coming apart, and Avni-Babad and Ritov's Study 3 shows the same interval running long in one paradigm and short in the other from a single manipulation. That years pass faster with age is repeated as settled. Measured, it is close to absent: Friedman and Janssen put age at about 1% of the variance in how fast adults say time is passing, and how rushed they feel more than seven times as strongly, on their own comparison. What does show an age effect is the single question about the last 10 years, which they suspect taps a belief about ageing rather than an experience of it. Laboratory timing points the other way. Older adults gave larger verbal estimates and shorter productions in Block, Zakay and Hancock's meta-analysis, a ratio 21% higher than younger adults, which means a given interval felt longer to them. Time slowing in danger is the most misreported of the three. Stetson, Fiesta and Eagleman did not find that perception speeds up. They found that the memory dilates while perception does not, and wrote that time-slowing is a function of recollection rather than perception. Nothing in the experiment supports the slow-motion camera picture. The oddball effect is often produced as laboratory proof of that picture, and Tse and colleagues invite the comparison in their first sentence while calling their own effect less dramatic. They report that an improbable item in a stream looks longer than an equally long probable one, with the distortion starting at least 120 milliseconds after onset and peaking at 225. Pariyadath and Eagleman then showed a tone's pitch and a flicker's rate are unchanged while the dilation is happening, so subjective time is not slowing in general, and traced the effect to prediction violation rather than salience. Fear and anxiety are also run together. Sarigiannidis and colleagues found induced anxiety shortening perceived durations, d = 0.68, and could not reproduce the lengthening under fear. James is quoted as the founder of the ageing claim, and his version was already a claim about memory: as experience turns into automatic routine, in his words, 'the days and the weeks smooth themselves out in recollection to contentless units, and the years grow hollow and collapse'.

sources.text: Block, R. A., & Zakay, D. (1997). Prospective and retrospective duration judgments: A meta-analytic review. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 4(2), 184-197. Read in full from the first author's posted copy at Montana State University; the source for the 20 experiments, d+ = 0.35 and the processing-difficulty ratios.

Block, R. A., Hancock, P. A., & Zakay, D. (2010). How cognitive load affects duration judgments: A meta-analytic review. Acta Psychologica, 134(3), 330-343. Read in full from the first author's posted copy; the source for the 117 experiments and the two paradigm effect sizes.

Block, R. A., Zakay, D., & Hancock, P. A. (1998). Human aging and duration judgments: A meta-analytic review. Psychology and Aging, 13(4), 584-596. Read in full from the third author's posted copy; the source for d+ = 0.40, the 1.21 age ratio and the per-method breakdown.

Friedman, W. J., & Janssen, S. M. J. (2010). Aging and the speed of time. Acta Psychologica, 134(2), 130-141. Read in full; the source for the 1,865 adults, the correlations with age and rushing, and for the description of Wittmann and Lehnhoff's variance figures.

Wittmann, M., & Lehnhoff, S. (2005). Age effects in perception of time. Psychological Reports, 97(3), 921-935. Abstract read at PubMed; the source for the 499 participants aged 14 to 94 and the at most 10% of variance. SAGE returned a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall notice on 21 September 2026, and OpenAlex and Unpaywall list no open copy anywhere.

Stetson, C., Fiesta, M. P., & Eagleman, D. M. (2007). Does time really slow down during a frightening event? PLoS ONE, 2(12), e1295. Read in full; the source for the 46-metre platform, the 31-metre fall, the 2.49 seconds, the 36% figure and the control comparison.

Avni-Babad, D., & Ritov, I. (2003). Routine and the perception of time. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 132(4), 543-550. Read in full from the second author's posted copy; the source for the Study 3 interaction and the Club Med field data.

Tobin, S., Bisson, N., & Grondin, S. (2010). An ecological approach to prospective and retrospective timing of long durations: A study involving gamers. PLoS ONE, 5(2), e9271. Read in full from the publisher's PDF; the source for the 116 gamers, the three session lengths and the 1.375 against 1.115 ratios.

Tse, P. U., Intriligator, J., Rivest, J., & Cavanagh, P. (2004). Attention and the subjective expansion of time. Perception & Psychophysics, 66(7), 1171-1189. Read in full from the publisher's PDF at SpringerLink, which is open; the source for the 120-millisecond latency and the 225-millisecond peak. An earlier note here said the full text was behind a login, which was wrong.

Pariyadath, V., & Eagleman, D. (2007). The effect of predictability on subjective duration. PLoS ONE, 2(11), e1264. Read in full from the publisher's PDF; the source for the unchanged pitch and flicker rate and for salience failing to enhance the dilation.

Sarigiannidis, I., Grillon, C., Ernst, M., Roiser, J. P., & Robinson, O. J. (2020). Anxiety makes time pass quicker while fear has no effect. Cognition, 197, 104116. Read in full from the Europe PMC full-text XML of PMC7033556; the source for the anxiety effect size and the two fear studies. The publisher's PDF at ScienceDirect returned a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall.

Wearden, J. H. (2015). Passage of time judgements. Consciousness and Cognition, 38, 165-171. Abstract read at PubMed; the source for the claim that passage judgements should be distinguished from duration judgements. ScienceDirect returned a Cloudflare bot challenge, and OpenAlex lists no open copy.

Droit-Volet, S., & Wearden, J. (2016). Passage of time judgments are not duration judgments: Evidence from a study using experience sampling methodology. Frontiers in Psychology, 7, 176. Read in full from the publisher's PDF; the source for the 27 participants, the absent age difference and the predictors of passage judgements.

Droit-Volet, S. (2019). Time does not fly but slow down in old age. Time & Society, 28(1), 60-82, published online 26 September 2016. Abstract read from the Crossref record. SAGE returned a Cloudflare bot challenge, and the two HAL records for the paper hold no file.

Arstila, V. (2012). Time slows down during accidents. Frontiers in Psychology, 3, 196. Read in full from the publisher's PDF; the source for the critique of the free-fall reading and for the realist account.

James, W. (1890). The Principles of Psychology, chapter XV, The Perception of Time, page 625. Read at Classics in the History of Psychology; the source for the quotation about routine and recollection.

Hammond, C. (2012). Time Warped: Unlocking the Mysteries of Time Perception. Canongate Books. Only the publisher's catalogue page was read, which lists the book as available in paperback published 2 May 2013 and in a second edition published 3 May 2012. The book was not obtained, it is not on archive.org, and the catalogue description does not use the phrase 'holiday paradox'.
